text.en: Asha cut a stem and saw rings. "Plants have an inner structure like us," said her teacher.

Plant tissues are grouped into three tissue systems. The dermal or epidermal system forms the outer covering, the ground tissue system forms the bulk of the plant and the vascular tissue system, with xylem and phloem, conducts water and food. Monocot and dicot roots and stems differ in the arrangement of these tissues.
Plastids are cell structures, and the chloroplast, with chlorophyll, is where photosynthesis takes place. Photosynthesis uses light, carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, and sunlight plays the key role. The light-dependent reactions occur at thylakoid membranes, often stacked as grana. Carbon fixation occurs in the stroma and uses products of the light-dependent reactions.
The plant also respires, taking in oxygen to release energy from food, and the chapter compares photosynthesis and respiration.

board.text: epidermal system

text.en: A cross-section shows tissues cut across an organ. Start by finding the outer layer, then look at the arrangement of tissues inside.

board.text: Anatomy studies structure

text.en: The epidermis is a covering layer. On a leaf, a waxy cuticle over much of the epidermis helps limit water loss.

board.text: The epidermis protects the surface

text.en: Some root epidermal cells extend into the soil as root hairs. These extensions increase the surface available to absorb water.

board.text: Root hairs increase contact with soil

text.en: Guard cells surround each stoma and help control its opening. Carbon dioxide can enter, while water vapour and oxygen can leave.

board.text: Stomata are openings in the epidermis

text.en: Ground tissue can store food or provide support. In a leaf, much of it contains chloroplasts and carries out photosynthesis.

board.text: Ground tissue fills much of the organ

text.en: Xylem carries water and minerals, chiefly from roots upwards. Phloem carries sugars from parts that supply them to parts that use or store them.

board.text: Xylem and phloem form conducting pathways

text.en: In a typical dicot root, xylem forms a star-like pattern with phloem between its arms. The pith is small or absent in many examples.

board.text: Compare roots using the centre

text.en: Xylem and phloem in a typical monocot root alternate around a central pith. Roots are compared using the whole arrangement.

board.text: A monocot root commonly has a broad pith

text.en: In a sunflower-type stem, vascular bundles form a ring around the central pith. Each bundle has xylem nearer the centre and phloem nearer the outside.

board.text: A typical dicot stem has bundles in a ring

text.en: In a maize-type stem, vascular bundles are scattered through the ground tissue, rather than forming a single ring.

board.text: Monocot stem bundles are scattered

text.en: Cambium between xylem and phloem can make new vascular tissue. Most monocot stem bundles do not have this layer.

board.text: Cambium allows thickening in many dicot stems

text.en: Many dicot leaves have closely packed palisade cells above a looser spongy layer. The air spaces in the spongy layer help gases move.

board.text: Compare leaf tissues as well as veins

text.en: In many monocot leaves, the veins run alongside one another. The mesophyll may not show distinct palisade and spongy layers.

board.text: Monocot leaves often have parallel veins

text.en: Look for chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes inside chloroplasts. Chlorophyll absorbs light that can drive photosynthesis.

board.text: Chloroplasts hold the photosynthetic machinery

text.en: A granum is a stack of thylakoids. The fluid region surrounding the stacks is called the stroma.

board.text: Grana are stacks and stroma surrounds them

text.en: Light-dependent reactions use energy from absorbed light. Splitting water during this stage releases oxygen.

board.text: Water supplies the released oxygen

text.en: In the stroma, the plant uses carbon dioxide and products of the light-dependent reactions to build carbohydrate.

board.text: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon for sugars

text.en: Carbon fixation does not directly absorb light. It can occur in daylight and depends on substances produced by the light-dependent reactions.

board.text: Dark reaction does not mean a night-only reaction

text.en: Living cells break down sugars. In aerobic respiration they use oxygen while producing carbon dioxide and water.

board.text: Respiration releases usable energy from food

text.en: Early sugar breakdown takes place outside mitochondria. Later steps in mitochondria supply much of the usable energy when oxygen is available.

board.text: Mitochondria are important for aerobic respiration

text.en: Without oxygen, some cells can obtain some energy by breaking down sugars through other pathways. Yeast fermentation is one example.

board.text: Anaerobic pathways release less usable energy

text.en: A plant can photosynthesise and respire together in suitable light. Respiration continues when the light is too weak for photosynthesis.

board.text: Day and night respiration continues

text.en: Compare a bundle arrangement to identify a stem. Then explain how leaf pores and chloroplasts support photosynthesis while plant cells also respire.

problem.en: Which vascular tissue carries water in a plant?

text.en: The vascular system conducts.
Xylem carries water.
So the vascular tissue system.

problem.en: Stem A has vascular bundles in a ring. Stem B has bundles scattered through the ground tissue. Which is the typical maize-like stem?

text.en: Stem B has scattered bundles.

why.en: Maize is a monocot, and this is a typical monocot stem arrangement.

text.en: Stem A is more like a typical dicot stem.

why.en: A ring of bundles surrounds the central region in many dicot stems.

problem.en: A leaf makes sugars in daylight. Why does it still need mitochondria?

text.en: Photosynthesis stores energy in carbohydrates.

why.en: Making carbohydrates and releasing energy from them are different processes.

text.en: Mitochondria support aerobic respiration, which supplies usable energy to cells.

why.en: Living leaf cells respire during the day as well as at night.

problem.en: Why is carbon fixation sometimes misleadingly called the dark reaction?

text.en: It does not use light directly.

why.en: It uses products supplied by the light-dependent reactions.

text.en: It can take place in daylight.

why.en: The term refers to the direct light requirement, not the time of day.

points.en: Three tissue systems: dermal, ground and vascular.
Xylem carries water, phloem carries food.
Chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis.
